At t=n/8, the 7 Hz samples are cos(2*pi*7n/8)=cos(2*pi*n-2*pi*n/8)=cos(2*pi*n/8). Periodicity and cosine evenness therefore give the exact 1 Hz sequence at every integer n. The other listed frequencies differ.
For integer n, cos(2*pi*9n/12)=cos(2*pi*n-2*pi*3n/12)=cos(2*pi*3n/12). Thus the reflected alias is 12-9=3 Hz, below the 6 Hz Nyquist frequency. Unit amplitude and zero phase agree as specified.

Twice the highest possible frequency is 2*6=12 samples per second. The question explicitly requires a rate strictly above that value, so 13 is the only listed choice. No assertion about sufficiency at the exact boundary is required.

answers.selected_option: Apply an analog low-pass filter before sampling that passes 3 Hz and removes 17 Hz.
answers.reasoning: At the stated sampling rate, 17 Hz folds to 20-17=3 Hz. For arbitrary phase the folded term is still a 3 Hz cosine with an appropriate phase, so samples alone cannot identify its origin in every case. Removing 17 Hz with the stipulated analog filter before sampling prevents that alias while retaining 3 Hz. Drawing or processing the already aliased sequence cannot supply the missing distinction.

Five values impose only finitely many constraints on an otherwise unspecified band-limited waveform; distinct such waveforms can agree at all five instants. Neither global uniqueness nor linear interpolation follows from those finite observations.

Standard DFT bin centres occur at f_k=k*f_s/N, so f_1-f_0=20/40=0.5 Hz. This uses the N-sample DFT interval convention, not the first-to-last sample span (N-1)/f_s, and does not promise two-tone resolution.
